note: Written by the reviewing agent. decision_check.py checks every step against the real code and attaches the real evidence results.

decisions.title: The crash is fixed

steps.text: the code took the first source line of a property with `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]`. A type from another library has none, so it crashed.
it asks a new helper, `GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(item)`, instead.
a second place now uses `FirstOrDefault()` so it gets nothing instead of crashing.
when there is no source line, the helper gives back nothing (`FirstOrDefault()?.GetSyntax()`).
two new tests check that the code is still produced (`Assert.Contains(expectedResolverHintName, hintNames)`).

decisions.verdict: The crash from the issue is fixed, and tests prove it.

because.text: The new tests fail before the change and pass after it.
Two of the tests still pass with the new filter taken out. So the crash fix alone makes them pass.

decisions.title: Some warnings are now silenced

steps.text: every warning went straight to `reportAnalyzerDiagnostic`.
every warning passes through `ReportIfLocatedInCompilation` first.
the warning points at code in this project (`IsInSource` and `ContainsSyntaxTree`),
it is shown to the user (`report(diagnostic)`).
it is dropped without a trace. The comment says the other library will report it (`reported by the compilation that defines them`).

decisions.verdict: This hides a warning users used to get, so the analyzer's owner must decide.

because.text: We wrote a small app that makes a common mistake. The old code warns about it. The new code says nothing, and no other place warns either.
Almost every warning in this file goes through the new filter, not only the one that crashed.

decisions.unsure: The comment assumes the other library reports the warning. Our test shows that, for a mistake in the app's own type, nobody does.
decisions.ask: Should these warnings be dropped, moved to the app's own code, or kept?

impact.who: Users whose own type sits inside a generic type from another library (a NuGet package or a built DLL).
impact.effect: A build error they used to get is gone, so the mistake is no longer caught at build time and can only surface when the app runs. The same filter covers 28 report sites with 19 kinds of warning, so more than this one case may go quiet.

decisions.title: The new notes promise too much

steps.text: the README says these warnings are `reported by the assembly that defines it`.
the warning page says the same: they are `reported by the project that defines that type`.
the code just drops them (`report(diagnostic)` runs only for this project's code).

decisions.verdict: The notes describe the hidden warnings as fine, so they wait on the owner's choice about the filter.

because.text: In our test, the mistake was in the app's own type. No other library warned about it. So the note is wrong there.

decisions.unsure: The notes may be right for mistakes that really live in the other library.
decisions.ask: If the warnings stay hidden, should these notes stay, or be changed?

impact.who: Maintainers and users who read the code comments.
impact.effect: Nothing changes at run time. But the notes say the hidden warnings are safe, so later readers may trust them and not look for the gap.

decisions.title: Old tests still pass

steps.text: every warning goes through the new filter (`ReportIfLocatedInCompilation`).
two places now use the safe helpers (`GetPropertyIdentifierLocation`, `FirstOrDefault()`).

decisions.verdict: No old test broke, but that does not prove the change is right.

because.text: All old tests in the project pass both before and after.

decisions.unsure: Old tests may not cover the warnings that are now hidden.

decisions.title: A real mistake now gets no warning

steps.text: the app's own type lacks the needed mark, so the code builds a warning (`TypeMustBeMessagePackObject`).
the warning points into another library, not this project (`ContainsSyntaxTree`),
it is never passed to `report(diagnostic)`, so the user sees nothing.

decisions.verdict: We found a hidden warning about the user's own code. Only a hand-written test could show it.

because.text: The old code warns about this case. The new code does not.

decisions.title: One change does two jobs

steps.text: the crash fix is small: a safe helper (`GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(item)`).
every warning is now sent through a filter (`ReportIfLocatedInCompilation`).
the issue asked only for the crash fix. The filter is extra (`private void ReportIfLocatedInCompilation`).

decisions.verdict: The filter is a separate change and should be judged on its own.

because.text: Almost every warning in the file goes through the filter.

decisions.title: One new test checks the filter

steps.text: the other library's type has a property with no key (`public int Unkeyed { get; set; }`).
the test `ClosedGenericStruct_FromMetadataReference_UnkeyedMember` expects no warning at all.
it passes only because the filter hides that warning (`RunWithMetadataReferenceAsync`).

decisions.verdict: This test locks in the hidden warnings, so it is not proof of the crash fix.

because.text: The test fails when only the filter is removed.

decisions.title: The filter also stops a second crash

steps.text: the other library is linked as a project, so a warning can point at a file outside this one (`not permitted to do`).
the warning was sent anyway (`reportAnalyzerDiagnostic`), and the analyzer crashed.
such a warning is dropped (`ContainsSyntaxTree`).

decisions.verdict: The filter does fix a real crash, so removing it needs a different fix in its place.

because.text: Our test cases with a linked project show the warning is now dropped instead of crashing.

decisions.title: A duplicate key still crashes

steps.text: two properties share one key in a type from another library (`KeysMustBeUnique`).
the analyzer still crashes, before and after the change. Its warning also goes through the filter (`this.reportDiagnostic?.Invoke`).

decisions.verdict: This crash is not fixed, but it is outside what the issue asked.

because.text: Our test cases tried this mistake on both versions.

decisions.title: Same count, different places

steps.text: one warning skips the filter (`reportAnalyzerDiagnostic?.Invoke`).
one more is sent a different way (`this.reportDiagnostic(deferred)`).
a simple text search also counts lines that are switched off (`////this.reportDiagnostic`).

decisions.verdict: Our count and the task notes agree on the number, by luck. We trust ours, made by a script.

because.text: The script counts only the lines that really run.

decisions.title: Extra work nobody asked for

steps.text: a filter was added (`ReportIfLocatedInCompilation`).
the README got a new section (`Generic types from referenced assemblies`).

decisions.verdict: The issue asked for no crash. The filter and the notes go beyond it.

because.text: The filter hides a warning the user needs.

decisions.title: The filter reaches too far

steps.text: every warning is wrapped, in one line (`diagnostic => ReportIfLocatedInCompilation`).
only two places crashed (`GetPropertyIdentifierLocation(item)`).

decisions.verdict: The filter touches far more than the crash needed.

because.text: Almost every warning in the file goes through the filter.
